title: Instruction Design & Evaluation
description: Make requirements explicit, measure results and respect trust boundaries.

lessons.title: Writing an Effective System Prompt
lessons.description: Treat the system prompt as the model's job description, not an afterthought.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: By the end of this lesson, you can name the key ingredients of an effective system prompt for a production LLM application.

sections.title: 📋 The system prompt is a job description
sections.content: A good system prompt typically states: the assistant's role and purpose, tone and style constraints, what it should and shouldn't do (scope boundaries), and how to handle situations outside its scope (e.g. 'if asked about topics outside X, say you can't help with that'). This connects directly to the prompt-engineering specificity principle from the generative AI course, applied to the one prompt that shapes an entire application's behavior.

sections.title: 🚧 Scope boundaries matter as much as capabilities
sections.content:
Explicitly stating what the assistant should *not* do is often as important as describing what it should do — a support bot without an explicit boundary can end up giving legal, medical, or financial advice it was never designed or vetted to give.

```python
system_prompt = (
    "You are a support assistant for Acme's billing system. "
    "Only answer questions about billing, invoices, and subscriptions. "
    "If asked about anything else, say you can only help with billing topics. "
    "Keep answers under 3 sentences unless the user asks for more detail."
)
```

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Writing a system prompt once and never revisiting it.** Real usage reveals edge cases and failure modes a system prompt should be updated to address — treat it as a living document, not a one-time setup step.

**Assuming a system prompt guarantees compliance.** It strongly influences behavior but isn't an unbreakable rule — determined or adversarial users can sometimes get a model to deviate from it (covered further in the eval-and-security track).

**Cramming unrelated instructions into one system prompt.** A bloated, unfocused system prompt is harder for the model to follow consistently than a focused one.

questions.question: What are the key ingredients of an effective system prompt for a production application?

options.text: Only a single sentence naming the company
The assistant's role and purpose, tone and style constraints, scope boundaries (what it should and shouldn't do), and how to handle out-of-scope requests
A complete list of every possible user question and its exact answer
System prompts don't need any specific structure at all

questions.explanation: A well-constructed system prompt covers purpose, tone, explicit scope boundaries, and a fallback behavior for out-of-scope requests — treating it as a genuine job description for the assistant.

questions.question: Why is explicitly stating what an assistant should NOT do often just as important as describing what it should do?

options.text: It's never important; only positive instructions matter
Without explicit scope boundaries, an assistant can end up responding to requests (like legal or medical advice) it was never designed or vetted to handle
Negative instructions always confuse the model and should be avoided
Scope boundaries only matter for creative writing applications

questions.explanation: Explicit boundaries prevent scope creep — without them, an assistant built for one purpose (like billing support) can end up improvising answers to sensitive topics well outside what it was designed and validated for.

questions.question: Why should a system prompt be treated as a living document rather than a one-time setup step?

options.text: System prompts should never be changed once deployed
Real usage reveals edge cases and failure modes that a static, never-revisited system prompt wouldn't have anticipated, so ongoing refinement matters
System prompts have no effect on production behavior once the model is deployed
Only the initial version of a system prompt is ever actually used

questions.explanation: Just as testing and monitoring in software development surfaces issues over time, real-world usage of an LLM application surfaces edge cases a system prompt should be updated to handle, making it something to iterate on rather than set once.

questions.question: In the example system prompt from this lesson, what happens if the user asks about something outside billing topics?

options.text: The assistant is instructed to say it can only help with billing topics
The assistant answers any question regardless of topic
The system prompt has no instruction for this case
The conversation ends immediately with no response

questions.explanation: The lesson's example system prompt explicitly instructs the assistant to say it can only help with billing topics when asked about anything else, illustrating a scope boundary in practice.

questions.question: How does this lesson connect writing a system prompt to the generative AI course's prompt-engineering material?

options.text: It applies the specificity principle from that course to the one prompt shaping an entire application's behavior
It says system prompts require a completely different, unrelated skill set
It claims specificity only matters for user-facing prompts, never system prompts
It says the generative AI course's material doesn't apply to system prompts at all

questions.explanation: The lesson explicitly draws a direct line from the prompt-specificity principle covered in the generative AI course to writing an effective system prompt for a production application.

questions.question: Why does the lesson caution against assuming a system prompt guarantees full compliance?

options.text: Because it strongly influences behavior but isn't an unbreakable rule — determined or adversarial users can sometimes get a model to deviate from it
Because system prompts have zero influence on model behavior
Because system prompts are only suggestions with no measurable effect
Because compliance is guaranteed as long as the prompt is under 3 sentences

questions.explanation: The lesson is explicit that a system prompt is a strong influence, not an unbreakable guarantee — this limitation is covered further in the eval-and-security track.

questions.question: Why does cramming unrelated instructions into one system prompt cause problems, according to this lesson?

options.text: A bloated, unfocused system prompt is harder for the model to follow consistently than a focused one
Unrelated instructions always improve the model's consistency
System prompts have no length limit so this is never actually a problem
Cramming instructions together always produces higher quality output

questions.explanation: The lesson's stated common mistake is packing too many unrelated instructions into a single system prompt, which makes consistent adherence harder for the model than a focused, well-scoped prompt.

questions.question: Why should a system prompt be treated as something to revisit rather than write once and forget, per this lesson?

options.text: Real usage reveals edge cases and failure modes a system prompt should be updated to address
System prompts are immutable once an application launches
Revisiting a system prompt after launch is technically impossible
Only the very first version of a system prompt is ever actually used by the model

questions.explanation: The lesson explicitly recommends treating the system prompt as a living document, since real-world usage surfaces edge cases worth addressing through ongoing refinement.

lessons.title: Define a testable prompt contract
lessons.conceptOverview: Specify the task, input boundaries, output format and handling of missing information. Examples demonstrate the desired pattern but do not update model weights. Separate trusted instructions from quoted input. A JSON request is not a guarantee: parse and validate the returned output against a schema.

sections.title: Practice
sections.content: Write a support-ticket classifier prompt with three labels and an unknown case. Provide one example per label and include a mixed-intent ticket in the test set.

sections.title: Review
sections.content:
Does asking for JSON guarantee schema-valid output?

No. Validate syntax and schema independently; use constrained output mechanisms when available, and test semantic correctness separately.

lessons.title: Evaluate prompt revisions
lessons.conceptOverview: Build a fixed dataset containing typical, ambiguous and adversarial inputs. Define a rubric before revising the prompt. Compare versions with the same model settings and record quality, latency and token usage. Use a development split for revisions and a held-out set for the final comparison; repeat stochastic trials when variability matters.

sections.title: Practice
sections.content: Compare an instruction-only classifier with one using examples. Score held-out inputs, inspect regressions, and reject changes that improve a single demo while hurting the agreed rubric.

sections.title: Review
sections.content:
Why keep evaluation examples separate from prompt-development examples?

Repeatedly tuning against the same examples overfits the prompt to that set. Held-out examples provide a more useful estimate of generalization.

lessons.title: Context boundaries and reliable explanations
lessons.conceptOverview: Place task-relevant context within a clear structure and define how to respond when evidence is absent or conflicting. Request concise explanations, citations or verifiable intermediate results when useful. Longer reasoning text is not proof of correctness. Treat retrieved text as data, and enforce permissions outside the model rather than relying on prompt wording alone.

sections.title: Practice
sections.content: Add a quoted document that says to ignore the task. Check that the output still follows the trusted instructions, and document the independent authorization check needed before any tool action.

sections.title: Review
sections.content:
Can a prompt alone enforce tool authorization?

No. The application must check the authenticated user intent, resource permissions and allowed actions before executing a tool.
